solution: A run of length x scores 100^(100^x), which dwarfs any number of shorter runs, so maximizing the score is exactly maximizing the multiset of run lengths sorted in non-increasing order lexicographically; and since selecting a cell never splits a run, every row that is black in at least one column should be used, which fixes the total length at the size of the union. Merging the two segment lists cuts the rows into independent blocks (maximal stretches covered by at least one column) whose scores simply add. Inside a block the rows black in exactly one column are forced to that column, so exactly one column switch must fall inside each maximal stretch of doubly-black rows that separates two forced stretches of different columns: the number of pieces is therefore fixed and each cut slides freely inside its own window, leaving the problem of choosing cuts t_i in disjoint ranges [a_i,b_i] so that the multiset of gaps is lexicographically largest. That is solved by repeatedly taking the piece that can be made longest -- pinning its left cut to the bottom and its right cut to the top of their windows -- and recursing on the two now independent sides, exploring every tied candidate because only adjacent candidates conflict (they share a cut); O((n+m)^2) with a two-pointer merge of the segment lists. The reduction and the recursion were checked against exhaustive search on several thousand small random grids and reproduce all four samples.
